annotations.keyFindings: 24 midwives and 16 women described a mismatch between fixed booking slots and fluctuating ward capacity, evening surges, midwives' distress and women feeling forgotten; both groups proposed capacity-linked booking and one point of contact.
annotations.limitations: Two units; women recruited through the units may under-represent those with the worst experiences.

annotations.keyFindings: 41 percent of 1,862 inductions started more than 12 hours late; delays were commoner on days with more than 5 inductions booked; on 23 percent of evening-surge shifts the ratio fell below one midwife to two women.
annotations.limitations: One unit; older data; 6 percent of timestamps missing.

claims.text: Midwives in two maternity units described a mismatch between fixed induction booking slots and labour ward capacity that changed from hour to hour.
claims.passage: Midwives described a mismatch between fixed booking slots and a labour ward whose capacity changed from hour to hour
claims.interpretation: The booking mechanism itself is a plausible source of delay and should be explored with booking clerks and bed managers as well as clinicians.

claims.text: On one labour ward, 41 percent of inductions started more than 12 hours after the booked time, and delays were more common on days with more than 5 inductions booked.
claims.passage: In total, 41 percent started more than 12 hours after the booked time.
claims.interpretation: Delay is common enough that a purposive sample of women with delayed induction is achievable.

claims.text: Women whose induction was delayed described feeling forgotten and receiving conflicting information about when it would start.
claims.passage: Women described feeling forgotten, receiving conflicting information about when induction would start
claims.interpretation: Communication while waiting is a candidate theme; uncertainty is high because the women were recruited through the units.

synthesis: Two retrieved records, appraised at abstract level, after the first search failed. A qualitative study in two units and two years of unit data describe the same mechanism: fixed booking slots meet fluctuating labour ward capacity, delays of more than 12 hours are common, evening surges strain staffing, and women feel forgotten while waiting. Neither study involved booking clerks or bed managers, and neither tested a redesigned booking system. The evidence is thin but consistent, and it supports a qualitative study that includes the people who run the booking process.
gradeRationale: Two single-setting studies, one qualitative and one observational, consistent in direction; limited by setting, recruitment through the units and missing timestamps.
summary: Two retrieved records appraised; three source-derived claims; overall certainty low.
